tinuerit iniurias quae sunt iustitiae contrariae. Expellere enim iniuriam iustam et arma iniqua: iustitiae est tali casu quod quovis moderamine inculpatae tutelae non in potestatate sub tali praetextu tunc enim videtur iniuriam magis inferre quam propulsare si alio modo suam tueri possit possessionem. Est igitur qui iniuste vult eicere iniuste ingrediendo vel armis vel sine armis cum non est ei aditus nisi per violentiam. Est et qui iuste possidentem vi iniuste eicit. Si autem possidens ei resistat qui operam implet ut possit eum in animo huius voluntate in aspersione non invadit nec ei obest contra vim iniuriam illam huius efficitur. Si autem qui dicit se possidere vim solum et cum viribus invaserit. Si regulariter verum est quod vis est quotiens quis quod detinet putat vi propulsare se posse. Licet autem de vi dicta ad praesens sufficiat. Si quis in aliquem metum induat eo videtur dum quid sit metus dicendum ne super hoc dubitari possit plenius. De primo remedio post disseisinam.
<margin>Incontinenti licet reicere quo modo respiciendo.</margin>
Si aliquis praedixit modo facta sit disseisina primum et principale competit remedium tale videlicet quod ille qui iniuste eicitur disseisitore praesente et si possit statim et sine intervallo dum tamen cuius sit aliquo intervallo flagrante disseisina vel maleficio recenti spoliantem Incontinenti est viribus repellere qui scit se ipsum possit vi et illata propulsare ille autem illata sine ad acta huius videtur: ut si aliter fieri non possit omnino hoc facit. Aliter enim videtur velle ipse magis uti et non iniuste utentem remittere possit abutendo creditur. Quod possum suum sic iniuste iuste petimus factum sua alius in utendo iniuste alieno nihil si possum iniusti adquiritur. Si autem ipsum nullo modo expellere potest ad superiorem auxilium erit recurrendum ut ea praestet vi et iurae quae res si autem olo vel quis impediunt ut non commode incontinenti repellat si si possit alioquin ad superiorem recurrat ut supra. Incontinenti autem quid sit videndum est quod tempus. Tempus autem non definitur sed per munitatem et animi et rei de quibus licet haec superius tractata sint. scilicet xv. dies quo cum ipse ad praesens non videtur videndum est utrum disseisitus praesens sit vel absens tempore disseisinae vel ipse sive canes vel eius paratus vel familia vel dum absens fuit alius ingrederetur in sua vacua possessione. In via dico corpore licet non animo. Si autem praesens fuit tempore disseisinae et hoc elegit ut incontinenti eicere non possit iocose disseisitorie. In hoc elegit ipse disseisitionem quod si velit persequere relicta via illa facta impetret adiectionem redire non poterit ad se ipsinam sua propria auctoritate resistere in praeiudicium superioris ad quem iam devoluta est cognitio. Si autem talem viam non elegerit fieri in estimo eadem die vel quanto ulterius cum debita gratia eodem quo si debuit primo die. Quod si primo die propter vim non potuit potest tamen in estimo aut incesto iures resistere. Arma quoque et auxilium amicorum convocare: quod si per longum tempus exspectaverit videbitur per hoc iniuriam dissimulasse et hoc illa parte alteri. Dictum est autem si possessor praesens vel familia praesens eicitur: nunc dicendum est si alias res eius et ipse esset ingredi per hunc vel per se latere vel quod de se posse repellere. Si autem absens fuerit

<column-break/>

quando cum vi cum venerationis vel pugnationis vel alia opportunitate distinguere locus distantiam temporis. Diligentia vel neglegentia secundum quod fuerit disseisitus in eodem comitatu vel in alio cum lege vel alibi dum tamen in regno non longe vel longius distinguatur. Quo ipse scire potuit disseisinam esse factam et quo tempore scivit. Ex quo casu inveniendo oportet unde sint rationabiles dietae ubi per se ei allocatus ditionibus et rationabilibus in quibus fieri diebus ut praedictum est ulterius et tunc videtur disseisitorie quod facit ex tunc incontinenti: animo autem et ex tunc sit faciendae. Ex quo post factam nuntium potuit eo modo si ad ex se regno impetratione simplici apud sanctum iacobum vel in servitio domini regis forte in gasconia dila-tionem habere debet de xlv. diebus et unum esse et tunc in mare. Similiter si ultra mare dies possit venire in regnum in xlv. diebus ut palam est ut vires resumat res. Si autem regnum in simplici peregrinatione ultra sanctum iacobum ad dilationem anni et diei et tunc ut palam est. Si autem generali passagio ad terram sanctam dabitur ei dilatio duorum annorum et xv. dierum tunc ut praedictum est. Et si aliter quis infra istos terminos fuerit ad disseisitore si necesse dominus rursus eum monuerit eadem modo rationabile passum quod per aliter via longinquam exspectanda absentia tunc valeat seoffatus si impetrare velit ut prius medio tempore et propter de vastatione perierit. Omnia autem qui mora fecerit longiorem quo ad restitutionem incontinenti factis ius sua dedisse videtur oblivioni. Prudenter igitur sibi ille quolibet iure in continenti flagrante disseisina in iniuriam disseisitoris praesentis dissimulavit. Neglegentia enim impetrandi. Desidiam vel ut eaque gerere impetratum non expectare per quod amittat veris possessionem naturalem videtur facilem. Et disseisitoris vani hinc incipiat ita quod si tunc eia non possit qui incontinenti quae ad quos ita debent monuerit videtur ex tunc praeplura. Tam oportet assisam a tunc non quod in quocumque tempore de hinc velit tot videtur ex tunc non videtur petere tibi remedia per assisam ut infra. Si autem ex tunc tunc monuerit flagrante disseisina non recuperato passum iam qui passus sum id quod fecit se ex tunc in omni-vancia et ego te possesionem iterum adhuc oportet et assisa si me ad seisinam recuperandam nec erit in omni-finitum quod per possesionem alios eadem possit monere a quo operatur et ipsum assisa. Et si tunc ipse assolia-tore conventa eadem possit spoliare facta non ope-rectori praestet disseisitoris qui per passus. Si autem versus possessor neglegens sine post disseisinam et neglegens in persequendo praestet dissimulavit in iniuriam. Impetret ordine ut de potentia respanis ut possit ex magis iustius re ad passum. Et si forte assisam reseruat et possessionem sua viribus utetur non iusto sed usurpare praesumit cum petit spoliationem post usurpationem assise non qui in re disseisitor sit. Si autem qui iusto et per neglegentiam vel divinam viam coepit possessionem naturalem videtur tamen et si neque dies hic velle regessum vis ut numquam dicitur in animo super petere. Si autem neque ad assisam redire qui primo ei operetur non poterit per assisam deinceps regiam impetrare sed super lege auxilium invocare qui in lege iustitiae lex in se quis ei optabit. For it is the part of justice to expel an unjust injury and wicked arms; in such a case, with whatever moderation of blameless defense [is used], it is not in the power [of the person] under such a pretext, for then he seems to inflict an injury rather than to repel one, if he could defend his possession in another way. Therefore, there is he who wishes to eject unjustly by entering unjustly, either with arms or without arms, when there is no access for him except through violence. There is also he who unjustly ejects one who is justly possessing. If, however, the possessor resists him who fulfills the operation so that he may be able to keep him in the intention of this will, in the act of scattering he does not invade, nor does he stand against him; that unjust violence is made his own. But if he who says he possesses, [acts] only with force and has invaded with forces. If it is regularly true that force is whenever someone thinks that he can repel by force what he holds. But let what has been said concerning force suffice for the present. If someone induces fear in anyone, it seems that what fear is should be said, so that there may be no doubt about this more fully. Concerning the first remedy after disseisin.

<margin>It is permitted to reject incontinently by looking at the manner.</margin>

If anyone, in the manner aforesaid, has committed a disseisin, the first and principal remedy is available, namely this: that he who is unjustly ejected, while the disseisor is present, and if he can, immediately and without interval—while it is yet fresh, by some interval of the disseisin or recent wrongdoing—is to repel the spoiler <term>incontinenti</term> <gloss>immediately/without delay</gloss> with force. He who knows himself [to be able to act] may repel what has been brought upon him by force; he who [repels] that which has been brought upon him, without the act, seems to do this: as if it could not be done otherwise, he does this altogether. For otherwise, he seems to wish more to use it himself and not to remit [the land] to one using it unjustly, [and] it is believed [he] is abusing it. That which we seek justly, because his [property] is his so unjustly, [and] another in using it unjustly acquires nothing of another's [property] if I am able [to stop] the unjust [acts]. But if he can in no way expel him, one must have recourse to the aid of a superior, so that he may provide those [remedies] which are of force and right. But if he or someone else impedes [him] so that he cannot repel [him] immediately, if he is able, otherwise he should have recourse to the superior, as above. However, it must be seen what "immediately" <term>incontinenti</term> <gloss>immediately</gloss> is, and what time [it involves]. Time, however, is not defined, but [is determined] by the immunity of both the mind and the thing, concerning which, although these things have been treated above, namely fifteen days—[concerning] which, since he is not present for the moment, it must be seen whether the disseised person was present or absent at the time of the disseisin, or he himself, or [his] dogs, or his equipment, or his household, or while he was absent, someone else entered into his empty possession. In the way, I say, [as to] the body, although not the mind. If, however, he was present at the time of the disseisin and chose this, so that he could not eject him immediately, [he is] facetiously [acting] as a disseisor. In this he chooses the disseisin itself, because if he wishes to pursue [it], having abandoned that way, [and] requests an addition, he will not be able to return to resist by his own authority in prejudice of the superior, to whom the cognizance has already devolved. But if he has not chosen such a way, it is estimated [to be] on the same day, or as much further with due grace, on the same day as he ought on the first day. But if, on the first day, he could not because of force, he can nevertheless resist in the estimation or in the interval of the law. He may also summon arms and the help of friends; but if he has waited for a long time, he will seem by this to have tolerated the injury, and this [applies] to the other part. It has been said, however, if the possessor is present or the family is present and is ejected: now it must be said if other things of his [are taken] and he himself were to enter through this [person] or through himself to hide, or what he might be able to repel from himself. But if he were absent

<column-break/>

when [he acts] with force, with veneration, or with fighting, or other opportunity, [one must] distinguish the place and the distance of time. [One must consider] diligence or negligence, according to whether the disseised person was in the same county or another, with law or elsewhere, provided that he is in the kingdom, not far or further, let it be distinguished. [One must consider] when he could have known that the disseisin was done, and at what time he knew it. From which case, upon finding [the facts], it is necessary [to determine] whence the reasonable days are [calculated], where [they are] allotted to him by his own authorities, and [the] reasonable [number of] days in which this may be done, as is aforesaid further, and then it is seen as a disseisin which he makes from then on <term>incontinenti</term> <gloss>immediately</gloss>; with the mind, [it is] to be done from then on. Since after the act he could have [sent] a messenger in that manner, if [he were] outside the kingdom by simple impetration [e.g., travel] to Saint James [of Compostela], or in the service of the lord king, perhaps in Gascony, he ought to have a delay of forty-five days, and one to be, and then [if] at sea. Similarly, if [he is] beyond the sea, [he may] come into the kingdom within forty-five days, as is plain, so that he may resume his strength. But if [he is] in the kingdom on a simple pilgrimage beyond Saint James, [he is entitled] to a delay of a year and a day, and then, as is plain. But if [he is] in a general passage to the Holy Land, a delay of two years and fifteen days will be given to him, then as aforesaid. And if someone else is within these terms [in relation] to the disseisor, if necessary the lord will warn him again in the same manner [that it is a] reasonable passage, which by another distant way the absence to be expected [would] then be valid, if he wishes to impetrate as before in the meantime, and because of devastation he will have perished. But all who have made longer delay than the restitution made <term>incontinenti</term> <gloss>immediately</gloss> seem to have given their rights to oblivion. Therefore, let him prudently [act] for himself by any right <term>incontinenti</term> <gloss>immediately</gloss>, while the disseisin is raging, [having] tolerated the injury of the present disseisor. For negligence in impetrating, sloth, or not expecting what has been impetrated [to be] done, by which he loses the natural possession of the truth, seems easy. And let [the case] of the vain disseisor begin here, such that if he cannot [act] then, [and] those who ought to be warned [are not], it seems from then on to be more than [enough]. So it is necessary that the <term>assisa</term> <gloss>legal session/jury</gloss> [be held] from then on; not that he wishes [to wait] for whatever time from here, [for] it seems he does not seek remedies for himself through the <term>assisa</term> <gloss>legal session/jury</gloss>, as below. But if he had warned from then on, while the disseisin was raging, [and] having not recovered the passage [he] already suffered, that which he did, he [did] from then on in all-vance <note>a scribal or archaic term for "fully"</note> and I [tell] you to possess again, [and] still it is necessary [to seek] the <term>assisa</term> <gloss>legal session/jury</gloss> to recover the seisin, nor will it be infinite that [he] can warn [others] through possession by which it operates, and the <term>assisa</term> <gloss>legal session/jury</gloss> itself. And if then he [the disseisor] himself, [having been] convened, is able to despoil [him], the act [is] not [provided] to the worker of the disseisor who suffered [the loss]. But if the possessor is negligent and [is] after the disseisin and negligent in pursuing, [and] has tolerated the injury, [he must] impetrate in order [for the matter] to proceed from the power of the response so that he may [proceed] more justly to the passage. And if by chance he reserves the <term>assisa</term> <gloss>legal session/jury</gloss> and uses his possession by forces, [he] is not presumed to usurp [it] justly, [for] when he seeks the spoliation after the usurpation of the <term>assisa</term> <gloss>legal session/jury</gloss>, [he] is not [one] who may be the disseisor in the matter. But if he who began [his] natural possession justly and through negligence or a divine way, yet [it seems] even if there is no day here [to] wish to [return] the way, as it is never said in the mind to seek [it] above. Item esto quod possessor ab disseisitore fecerit statim et eodem die quo disseisitus fuit spoliatum. ad alium transferat rem: queritur an possit ille ad quem res translata est incontinenti eia auctore domino disseisitore sicut ipse primus principalis disseisitor: et videtur quod sic. Dum semper sit retenta civilem possessionem quousque naturalem amiserit. Eodem modo si passim non disseisitus velit agere ipsum uti recuperabit. quia ubi fecit ei disseisinam principalis. primus disseisitor abstulit ei naturalem possessionem. secundus autem et res quietas simul ab alio abstulit et utrumque amiserit. et naturaliter et civiliter videtur contra sic alio respondere. Si enim unus primus tenetur ex disseisina tam ad penam et ius ad restitutionem quod non est in re. et secundus ad sedem ut tenet adhuc rem ad penam quia ad restitutionem. ad penam quia abstulit civilem possessionem ad restitutionem quia habet rem que debet restitui. Sed quid si primus post disseisinam per longum intervallum transtulerit ad alium inperitum. et ubi primus principalis disseisitor non tenet ad penam per inuriam tunc ad quem res spiritualis translata sunt an ad restitutionem secundum virtutem assise ut infra dicetur. Item esto quod primus disseisitor post disseisinam suam sine ab alio disseisitus fuerit utrique dominus si voluerit ulciscit disseisinam in continenti eiceat eum post intervallum per pacem videtur. Et eodem modo si per assisam ubi agere poterit usus vana age usque ad iusticiarium presentem. si autem ad tempus dissimulaverit poterit ille primus disseisitor in suam disseisinam revertere si agere velit passim possessionem ab invicem motu propria sicut et impeditus laboribus et plus de se si fecerit aliquo quo ille secundus in possessione se querit de recenti perrexit. an videtur de iure se intruisse videtur. quod sic minus quid dicitur sicut si ad aliud tempus non impune nec debet se ingerere ex officio suo si non potuerit disseisire quod si fecerit cadit in assisam. si videtur de vi et sine iusticia et violentia per regem iusticiarium ut in imposita vi autem in imposita de no inmittat ad alium inestimat ne ineat in assisam ne si aliquis alius disseisitus iniuste redisseisitus ad hoc invadat ut disseisitionem suam inmanem trahat si vi eum disseisia que iusta est amoverit tunc disseisitoris in impositam sustineat cadit in assisam. si alius qui venit ut iuste possidentem per vim deiciat ai possidens in possessione vi plie agat et se defendat. et vi eum inuasoris in impositam sustineat. cadit omnino in assisam. Dictum est supra quomodo disseisitus poterit disseisitorem suum incontinenti reicere in primis ubi qui vim detinuit civilem possessionem. sive aliter dicendum est quod recurritur ad superius auxilium ai utrumque amiserit possessionem naturalem videlicet et civilem. Cum igitur disseisitus ita negligens fuit in hac parte quod noluit vel non posset disseisitorem suum reicere de tenencia propria sua et ei per negligeniam. as no dis. multas vigilias et cogitacionem in iuvencia recuperande possessionis quia cum disseisitus iniuste amiserit sicut in do uero per summam omnium coin abis magis iuris sollempnitate qui propter negotium eminet loci a' uo solum hie vi assisam in rebus corporalibus sive in iuribus sicut iuribus et parit ad tenentia sicut de iure pascendi fodiendi nisi sic iustius appetit. Est autem ista recognitio sive assisa ex pluribus iunctis in lapis ut infra de restitutione dampnorum. Et si plures persequitur cuiusque disseisitorum pro sua tam quod se fecit. persequi enim ad penam et inuriam persequitur et cui quo ad restitutionem. Item videtur et propter actoris persequi et qui omnes pro quindium ad hoc agunt duos pro ut plures eodem tempore res ad ipsos pervenit per unam disseisinam vel post disseisinam per translationem statim ut postquam persequitur in quindium vnus pro quindium ad penam si fatur in inuriam etiam pro quindium ad restitutionem ai iam detineat. quare nulla sunt alia poterit respondere per se quod disseisitor non sit quid ipse aliter licet tenent ad penam. nec eam detinet licet possit restituere: nullam inuriam fecit. Convictus est vtrique pro in una tunc deinde peccat passim a uno alio. persequitur vbi plures per quindium ad penam et plures quindium ai ad restitutionem secundum quod res in plures manus devenerit post disseisinam vel secundum quod in plura capita ipsa disseisina divisa fuit et partita. Adquiritur vero passim ipsam non solum in re spoliata corporali: verum etiam in fructus medio tempore percepti. Item non solum ipsa res. scilicet in ipsa re per rames. sed non solum ipsa res. scilicet in libras et per lucris evanuerit. de quibus mico facta est in phap. Item quia ad omnis non pervenit vi querela quindium ius inpossessione fuerit videndus est quis au oportet remedium passim ad quem pertineat querela an si detineretur res ad quod non pertineat. et sciendum quod ad eum ad eosque la quod nomine suo pro tenuerit et in alieno. Sive adulti sine in fodo. scilicet non ad terminum annorum licet ad vitam et medium. ...with forces and right, [the] law does not aid him in his right, because if he could, he would not, and if he would, he could not. In the same way it answers him unless he has a just and sufficient impediment. Item, let it be that the possessor, immediately and on the same day on which he was disseised, has despoiled [the property] and transfers the thing to another: it is questioned whether he to whom the thing was transferred may [act] <term>incontinenti</term> <gloss>immediately</gloss>, with the lord disseisor as author, just as the first principal disseisor himself: and it seems that he may. Provided that the civil possession is always retained until he has lost the natural [possession]. In the same way, if he is not disseised, [and] wishes to act, he will recover it himself. Because where he made the disseisin to him, the first disseisor took away his natural possession. The second, however, and the quiet things [he] took away from another at the same time, and both [he] lost, both naturally and civilly, it seems [to] answer against him thus. For if one, the first, is held by reason of disseisin, as much for the penalty as [for] the right of restitution, which is not in the thing, and the second [is held] to the seat [of the court] as he still holds the thing, for the penalty [and] for the restitution; for the penalty because he took away the civil possession, [and] for the restitution because he has the thing which ought to be restored. But what if the first, after the disseisin, through a long interval has transferred [it] to another ignorant [person], and where the first principal disseisor is not held to the penalty by the injury, then [concerning] him to whom the spiritual things were transferred, whether [he is held] to restitution according to the virtue of the <term>assisa</term> <gloss>legal session/jury</gloss>, as will be said below. Item, let it be that the first disseisor, after his disseisin, has been disseised by another: [to] both, the lord, if he wishes, avenges the disseisin <term>incontinenti</term> <gloss>immediately</gloss>, [he] may eject him after the interval by peace, it seems. And in the same way, if [he acts] through the <term>assisa</term> <gloss>legal session/jury</gloss>, where he will be able to act, he uses a vain [process] until [he reaches] the present justice. But if he has tolerated it for a time, that first disseisor may return to his disseisin if he wishes to act, [having] the possession from each other by his own motion, just as he was impeded by labors, and more of himself if he has done [something] whereby that second [disseisor] seeks himself in the possession, [and] has proceeded recently. Whether it seems [he has] intruded himself by right [or not] is seen. That so [it is] less [certain] what is said, as if [he does not act] at another time [it is not] without impunity, nor ought he to insert himself from his office if he cannot disseise, for if he has done so, he falls into the <term>assisa</term> <gloss>legal session/jury</gloss>. If it is seen [he acts] by force and without justice and violence by the king's justice, as [when] force is imposed, [and] it is not imposed again, [he] may not admit to another [the claim] so that he may not enter into the <term>assisa</term> <gloss>legal session/jury</gloss>, lest if any other [person who is] disseised unjustly [is] re-disseised, he invades [in order] to draw his own immense disseisin [out], if he has removed by force him who is just, then [he] sustains the [penalty] of the disseisor's imposed [force] and falls into the <term>assisa</term> <gloss>legal session/jury</gloss>. If another who comes [in order] to cast out the justly possessing [person] by force, [and] the possessor [is] in possession, he acts by force and defends himself, and [the invader] sustains [the penalty] of his own force imposed, he falls entirely into the <term>assisa</term> <gloss>legal session/jury</gloss>. If, however, he defends himself against him who [uses] force against the justly possessing [person] in his possession, so that the just possessor ejects [him] without [delay] and resumes his possession with a mindful heart, so that he was required [to use] force [and] had civil force, he sustains [the penalty] if it is just; this is [what] he has, namely, he possessed [it] justly, [with] civil possession, until it was lost through negligence, impotence, or desperation. In the case of force, the last [one] does not admit [the other] again and requires that he may not invade into the <term>assisa</term> <gloss>legal session/jury</gloss>. Item, [concerning] all things done because of force as a friend uses force from his office [and] by the peace of the lord king. And finally, it is to be noted that [concerning] the expertise to be made, all [things] are not distinct because of the intervals where someone was unjustly disseised; [one] ought [to use] the <term>assisa</term> <gloss>legal session/jury</gloss> [and] ought to reject the disseisor <term>incontinenti</term> <gloss>immediately</gloss>, if he can; if, however, [he cannot]...

<column-break/>

...he ought not to recede therefrom, and he ought to strike continuously; and because he has receded once through impotence, he does not lose the possession, because after the time he will not be able to return to eject [him], nor [to exercise] the seisin, because thus he loses it by his own will [and] resumes [it] to the hands of the superior, as it is devolved into cognizance. It is necessary, therefore, of necessity to have recourse to the superior, just as the inferior seeks [him]. Item, for the present, concerning the rejection [of those] joined [in disseisin], these things suffice as an example.

Or otherwise it is to be said that he has recourse to superior aid if he has lost both [kinds of] possession, namely natural and civil. Since, therefore, the disseised person was so negligent in this part that he would not or could not reject his disseisor from his own holding, and through negligence [he has] no disseisin [claim], [he must employ] many vigils and thought in the effort of recovering possession, because when the disseised person has lost unjustly, as in the true [case] by the sum of all [the law], [one proceeds] more by the solemnity of right which [is used] because of the business [which] emerges from the place, [and] solely [because of] this force, the <term>assisa</term> <gloss>legal session/jury</gloss> [is granted] in corporeal things or in rights, just as [other] rights, and [it] applies to the holding just as concerning the right of pasturing or digging, unless [he] seeks [it] more justly. This recognition or <term>assisa</term> <gloss>legal session/jury</gloss> is [composed] from several things joined in the stone, as below concerning the restitution of damages. Nulli autem competit qui in seisina fuerit nomine alieno quia talis non possidet licet sit in seisina: sicut procurator. auctor. procurator. aut custos. firmarius sive fructuarius nomine firme suae. Item servus sive alienus. id est servus vel alius quicunque alius: ut non competit assisa nomine dominorum qui sasina iniusta habent per disseisinam vel inquisitionem rerum ab eis disseisitis sive qui in seisina fuerunt domino faciente sicut extra eum ab eo qui ius in re habet dicitur. Item assisa non competit heredibus de medio passis antequam videtur prima facie quod non. cum disseisitor per se habeat in assisa ut videtur in exceptionem videlicet quod alius disseisitus non videtur nisi teneatur sasina ad quam ipse non potuit per iniuriam male fecerit in ubi rem. Sed si servus licet talis iniuste possidens nec nullam habet actionem vel ius non debet habere ei querela remedium passim et tales qui ius non habent per commodum possessoris nisi cum eis nullam habent exceptionem contra sasinam ut ubi eum per modum possessoris dico quod si tales qui ius non videntur ei sasinam peterent: nunquam recuperarent ius possidendi quominus in iuste ad eandem operetur in herede. Item remaneret suo loco possidendi. Cum igitur ad eandem non habeat realem quamvis iniuste possideret disseisitus ad primam recuperare non possent. Si talis petat passim res ei de iure non competit: cum in modum disseisine praedicte quod praedicti disseisitores nulla sasina hic petunt ex quo non. Item competit remedium passim et querela ei ad se titulum habuit in se omnes a quibus feoffatus fuit domino vel domino. et ius enim qui in se ius rei quaeritur in se ut si quis a vero domino auctoritate sua propria qui ad eam tenuit tenuit annos. ut ab eo qui in gratia videtur per disseisinam vel in sessionem sit talis feoffatus per aliquod tempus in pace tenuit: a vero domino etiam si petat si vi ruit. dum cum alii sit quod sufficit pro se pro titulo a vero domino vero feoffatore ad titulum ab eo tenet etiam non potest per titulum a feoffamento ad se suum licet quod non inveniat nam in ex a vero domino cum possit rumpere si quod per sufficiens titulo non invenit. Item competit remedium per ius taco passim ei qui orio su aliquo titulo in seisina fuit per disseisinam vel inquisitionem a sua non sunt disseisiti dum tamen quod tenet quod sufficiat pro titulo usus omnis sive tenet ius sive non. x. annorum unde possit aliquando tempus sive annorum. Item competit querela et remedium passim haec quis eiectus non fuit per vim sed per paupertatem. Si autem nemine in sasina relicto. a sasina recessit et alii res ius suum non adnuntiat ut repellat. Item competit querela et remedium passim si quis in alieno vi voluerit cum ius non habeat ex domino voluntate. Et eodem modo si dominus non permiserit ut infra ut patet est supra in principio. Item competit ei querela et remedium per assisam si quis disseisitus fuerit ab aliquo per vim qui sic tenuit. Item competit ei querela et remedium passim qui suspensus est ut metum aspe sit ei qui est sane mentis dum etiam in ad quisitione tene-

menti videtur sana mentem quod ex quo semel dum sane videtur creaverit animum hunc retinendi id ius fuerit in vi furore si pervenerit animum mutare potuit. nec desinit possidere quamvis se nase a possit nec disseisire. nec desinit possidere per id amittere non potuit per aliquem cuius tempore id quod tempore pro illo dilucidis gaudet intervallis adquisierunt. Item oportet tamen ei qui feodi firmarius est qui ei qui tenet in feodo vel ad vitam. Et eodem modo competit ei qui tenet in solagio per servitium reddendi sive ei qui tenet per viam militarem. Item competit vobis de re si tibi data ad vitam. ut eos qui praeter matrimonio quominus donum mutari possit et post feodum. Si qui vero post mortem donatoris in sasinam sint sine vobis disseisiri non possit dum autem quod alibi sufficit pro titulo invenit. Item oportet ei per obitum in statu liberi si post mortem patris sasinas et imposuit ubi alias ex duorum potestate. Si autem sub potestate duorum a feoffato fuit sive a domino sive ab extraneo competit ei assisa versus omnes. And indeed, if anyone ejects those who were in <term>sasina</term> <gloss>seisin/possession</gloss> in the name of lords, the assize <note>a legal proceeding to recover land</note> belongs to the lord, specifically for recovering his seisin. However, it belongs to no one who was in seisin in another’s name, because such a person does not possess, even if he is in seisin, such as a proctor, an author, a proxy, or a guardian, a farmer <note>a tenant of land</note> or a usufructuary in the name of his farm. Likewise, a servant or another person, that is, a servant or anyone else whatsoever, so that the assize does not belong to them in the name of lords who have unjust seisin through disseisin or an inquisition of things disseised from them, or who were in seisin while the lord was acting, just as it is said of one who has a right in the thing outside of him <note>i.e., someone claiming a right against the current possessor</note>. Likewise, the assize does not belong to heirs who have passed through the middle <note>an intermediary</note> before it is seen at first glance that it does not. Since the disseisor has it for himself in the assize, as is seen in an exception, namely that another disseised person is not seen unless he is held by the seisin to which he himself could not [reach] through injury, he did evil where the thing is. But if a servant, even if such a one possesses unjustly and has no action or right, should not have a remedy of complaint everywhere, and such as those who have no right through the convenience of the possessor, unless they have no exception against the seisin, as where I say that through the mode of a possessor, if such persons who are not seen to have a right were to seek seisin from him, they would never recover the right of possessing, any more than he works unjustly toward the heir. Likewise, he would remain in his place of possessing. Since, therefore, he does not have a real [action] toward it, although he might possess unjustly, the disseised person could not recover to the first. If such a person seeks a complaint, the thing does not belong to him by right, since in the mode of the aforesaid disseisin, the aforesaid disseisors seek no seisin here since they do not. Likewise, a remedy of complaint belongs to him who had the title in himself, [and] all from whom he was enfeoffed to the lord or the lord; and the right, indeed, which is sought in the thing, is in him as if someone [holds it] from a true lord by his own authority, who held it for years, as from one who is seen to be in grace through disseisin or a session, such a person is enfeoffed for some time and held it in peace; even from the true lord, if he seeks it, even if he rushes in by force, while it is sufficient for him for a title from the true lord as the true feoffor, he holds it by title, even if he cannot [claim] by title from the feoffment to his own [right], although he might not find it, for in [that] from the true lord, since he can break it if he does not find it by a sufficient title. Likewise, a remedy belongs by the right <unclear>taco</unclear> <note>likely *tacito* or *tacito jure*, by silent right</note> to him who was in seisin by some title through disseisin or an inquisition, provided that they are not disseised from theirs, provided that what he holds is sufficient for a title, whether he holds the right or not, of ten years, from which he might sometimes have time or years. Likewise, a complaint and remedy belong to him who was not ejected by force but through poverty. But if, with no one left in seisin, he receded from the seisin and does not announce his right to the other thing, so that he may repel [the claim]. Likewise, a complaint and remedy belong to him if someone wishes to be in another’s [land] by force, when he has no right from the lord's will. And in the same way, if the lord has not permitted it, as is clear above in the beginning. Likewise, a complaint and remedy by assize belong to him if anyone has been disseised by someone by force who held it in such a way. Likewise, a complaint and remedy belong to him who is suspended, so that he might be in fear of him who is of sound mind, provided that even in the acquisition he holds—

<column-break/>

it seems he is of sound mind, because from the time when he appeared to be sane he created the intent to retain this right, [and] if he arrived in the frenzy of force, he could have changed his intent. He does not cease to possess, although he can neither be sane nor disseised. Nor does he cease to possess, so he could not lose it through anyone in whose time he acquired it during those intervals of lucidity. Likewise, it is necessary, however, for him who is a fee-farmer <note>a holder of land for rent</note>, [and] for him who holds in fee or for life. And in the same way, it belongs to him who holds in <term>solagio</term> <gloss>ground-rent/tenure</gloss> by the service of rendering, or to him who holds by military way. Likewise, it belongs to you regarding the thing if it was given to you for life, so that those who, apart from marriage, [prevent] the gift from being changed and after the fee. If there are any who are in seisin after the death of the donor without you, you cannot be disseised, provided that elsewhere it is found sufficient for a title. Likewise, it is necessary for him through death to be in the state of a free person if he imposed seisin after the death of his father, where otherwise [he was] out of the power of two. Likewise, he who belongs to the villain <note>a serf or unfree tenant</note> is solemnly in the lord king's demesne if he harms the borough, that is, concerning the fine, outside as from the court, by white rents <note>payments in silver</note>, ten years, concerning pleas in their Gloucester, in the year of King Henry the Fourth, an assize of novel disseisin, if there are several of the heir. Likewise, it belongs to a free person who holds <term>villenagium</term> <gloss>villein tenure</gloss> by customary villein service, or if he was coupled to a villein woman on land that he held elsewhere, even if, notwithstanding that he held <term>villenagium</term>, he was coupled to a villein woman. Likewise, it belongs to him who was enfeoffed by someone who held for life in your name if he drives a pledge, or for a term, or in any other way as in the fairs [or] the place of pleas. Likewise, it belongs to a villein in his case by the right of the lords of others, while they are under power, until he ejects him as is said. But if he was under the power of two, by a feoffee, or by the lord, or by a stranger, the assize belongs to him against all. But if from a stranger, the assize belongs to him against all, then by his own use to his grandson while under their power, if by chance he wishes to disseise him. Likewise, it belongs to him who held the thing until it was pending, just as another who has free [tenure] holds, who can be [disseised] to you, who would never be pending to him, so he can remain in the whole fee of heaven <note>a likely scribal error or metaphorical flourish for the entirety of the estate</note>. Likewise, an assize belongs if to two, either to you successively at different times, or if they can be in seisin at the same time, or to you the right and the donor's pacts, [and] from here another's seisin to your other. But if the seisin is not from the father, he is not ejected, so he should not receive [it]. escapes His yoke, at which, being despised, He might be indignant and grow angry. Nor is there anything wiser than Him that might strike emulation into Him. Therefore, since these things do not happen to Him, nothing remains of His nature except the good itself. Just as, however, none of those things that are evil are contained in Him, so the good is not found in any other. For in individuals, other things are individuals, both in small things, in great things, and even in those which are according to one, and in that greatest and most powerful animal of all, which indeed fills the things begotten with passions. For generation is a certain passion; where there is passion, however, the good is not placed in any way. Where there is good, no passion is placed. Where there is day, there is in no way night; where there is night, neither is there day. Therefore, the good cannot exist in generation. It remains, therefore, that it is in that which is unbegotten. Just as, however, participation in all things is granted to matter, so also the world is good by participation in the good; I say good, in so far as it also makes all things. In which part the world is indeed good; in all remaining things, it is not good. For it is passive and movable, and furthermore the cause of all passions. In man, moreover, by comparison to evil, it is good. For that which is not too much evil, but also less evil, we call good among men. From which it happens that our good is nothing other than the smallest portion of evil. From where it also follows that the good of this kind cannot be separated from evil. For this good pollutes with the admixture of evils; the good, however, does not remain further infected. If it does not remain at all, it makes evil. In God alone, therefore, does the good itself exist. Wherefore, let the name of the good be present to man alone, O Asclepius; the nature of the good, by no means. For the material body, finished everywhere and oppressed by depravity, labors, pains, desires, wrath, deceptions, and foolish opinions and trifles, cannot grasp it. I consider it the worst of all, however, O Asclepius, that each one of those things which I have said is believed to be the highest good. Iura quibus uictis dedimus: quibus arua, domosq;
Præbuimus: Lydos, Asiæq; uberrima uastant

Nec duce, nec numero freti, sed inertia nutrit,
Prodigiumq; ducum: quorum per crimina miles
Captiuus dat terga suis: quos teste subegi

Aula choris, epulisq; uacat: nec perdita curant:
Dum superest aliquid. nequid tamen orbe reciso
Venditor amittat. prouincia quæq; superstes
Diuiditur: geminumq; duplex passura tribunal,
Cogitur alternis pretium sarcire peremptæ.
Sic mihi restituunt populos. hac arte repertæ

<vocab>Eutropius, Claudian, Bistoniis, Araxe, Antiochi, Caucasus, Phasis, Gothunni, Lydos, Danubio, Mineruæ</vocab>
translation:
The nations exult with merit, and we, now easy prey,
Are to the Bistones and the snowy tribes.
The rising expanse will grow foul, the plows having been driven out.
Alas for me, what cities, and in what time of Mars,
Ignorant of war, they have seized in a single course!
Recently, the cavalry coming from the furthest Araxes
Terrified the walls of Antioch: and the very head of beautiful
Syria was nearly consumed by hostile flames.
And as it rushes, heavy with spoils, and with nothing hindering,
Happy in the slaughter: the continuous wound follows
With a second blade: nor does the Caucasus now send me enemies,
Nor does the icy Phasis: wars are born in the very
Bosom. The Roman legion of old, the Gothunni
To whom we gave rights when conquered; to whom we provided
Fields and homes; they lay waste to the Lydians and the richest parts of Asia
With fires: and if any part remained from the first tempest.
Relying on neither leader nor number, but sloth nourishes them,
A prodigy of leaders: through whose crimes the captive soldier
Turns his back to his own: those whom I subdued with the
Danube as witness: and he fears a part, who repelled them all.
The court is empty of dances and feasts: nor do they care for what is lost:
While something remains. Yet, lest the seller lose anything
With the world cut to pieces. Every surviving province
Is divided: and about to suffer the double tribunal,
It is forced to make up the price of the destroyed one in turns.
Thus they restore the peoples to me. By this art, they find
Ways to increase the number of rulers while the lands perish.
In you now is my only hope. Instead of the leaf of Minerva,
I hold out these tears to you. Succor the falling.
Snatch me away at last. Snatch me away from servile kingdoms.

translation:
It will be meager. I will follow the ancient deeds and your first youth:
The present leads the mind to itself.
I might narrate justice. The glory of Mars shines out.
I might recount the strengths of the armed man. He did more unarmed.
That Latium flourishes. That Africa, restored to Latium, serves:
That Iberia does not know the neighboring Moor:
That Gaul, safe, marvels at the unwarlike Rhine.
Shall I sing of the Thracian Angelida, and the labored struggles
With the Hebrus as witness? A great sea is opened to me:
And the Pierian chariots themselves grow weary with the steep
Road of countless praises. For indeed, ever since
The earth began to be tilled by mortals: never has a pure
Lot of good things been granted to any man. Whom a face honors:
Manners disgrace. Whom a more beautiful soul adorns:
The body abandons. That one is more distinguished in wars:
But he fouls peace with vices. Fortunate in public matters:
But less so in private. Single things ennoble each one:
One is favored by handsome form, one by strength in arms,
One by rigor, one by piety, another by skill in law,
One by offspring, and chaste marriage beds are scattered among all:
In you they flow mixed together: and what separate things
Make men blessed: you hold collected. Why should I revolve deeds?
And the military service of a father? Whose fame, if he had
Done nothing famous: and his faithful right hand had not led
The red-haired wings in strength: would be enough for his son Stilicho.
An arduous mind always, even from a boy, and it shone in tender years.
The honor of a greater fortune. Upright, and keen,
To attempt nothing short: to cling to no thresholds
Of the powerful: and already speaking things worthy of future annals:
